subsubtopic: DISTRIBUTION BY STATISTICS CANADA OF SURVEYS TO SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Statistics Canada
reports that: Commercial businesses with less than 20 employees, and with relatively small total revenues and sales are classified as "small" business for statistical purposes. To minimize the response burden for them, Statistics Canada provides small businesses with abbreviated survey questionnaires. In addition, the use of sampling in some surveys means that reliable information on all small firms can be obtained by surveying only 5 per cent to 15 per cent of the total, the sample size depending on the particular survey in question. Over the years 1968 to 1972 inclusive, the average number of different surveys designed to collect data from small firms varied from 56 to 59. Most questionnaires are designed for surveys of specific industries and the maximum number of Statistics Canada surveys a small firm engaged in a single activity would be subject to in one year is four. Periodically, Statistics Canada asks some of the smaller firms for information on the nature, location and organization of their business in order to maintain its survey mailing lists and reporting structures up to date.

increase in the membership of the House of Commons to 299.
I might make one further comment. At one time a member of the House of Commons represented, on the average, about 40,000 persons. Today, if no changes are made, the number of persons represented per member is in excess of 80,000. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) for his generosity in allowing me to speak today.

There have been, over the past few weeks, questions addressed to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) relating to the effects of rent increases in various public and subsidized housing projects. This question has arisen, apparently, as a result of the announced increase in the old age pension, and I should like to pursue this matter briefly this afternoon, particularly since these increases in rents are justified under some of the provisions of the National Housing Act. I have been looking through the act trying to find these provisions. I know they are there, although I have not been able to find them all. I know that section 15 provides for CMHC to approve increases in rents in cases where the cost of maintaining buildings built directly by CMHC or with CMHC approved money have risen.
We, in this corner of the House, have addressed a number of questions to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs relating to this matter, and we have received a number of answers. This afternoon I should like to go into that subject again briefly, to see if we can obtain anything like a complete picture as to what is happening in that sector. Obviously, a considerable number of our senior citizens are being sorely affected by these increases in rents, and others are feeling insecure indeed, because they feel their turn may come at any time. It is important to raise this point, because a good number of people are beginning to question the generosity and, indeed, the
March 21, 1973

integrity of the state, inasmuch as the federal government offers an increase in pensions on the one hand, and provincial or municipal governments take much of these pension increases away in rent increases on the other hand.
As I suggested a moment ago, we have asked the government some questions on this, and have received a fair number of answers. I do not say that those answers are in contradiction to one another; at the same time, they do not give us a complete picture. One answer is to this effect: that the minister has ordered that there be no rent increases in CMHC owned buildings as a result of the increase in the old age pension; in other words, that the rents in CMHC owned buildings will be frozen for a period of time. This is all very good, Mr. Speaker, but we have experienced difficulty in finding out how many buildings are directly owned or controlled by CMHC. Central Mortgage and Housing itself is not directly a landlord in many projects housing senior citizens in this country. So far as I can tell, CMHC is the landlord in those cases where it has received into its hands properties and houses whose owners have fallen into default on mortgage payments. As it has those houses in receivership it is, in effect, the landlord. I do not think many senior citizens inhabit those houses. I also understand that CMHC is either the landlord or in direct control of a number of buildings in the far north, in the Northwest Territories. I also understand that the only project CMHC controls directly as owner is Habitat in Montreal. How many senior citizens live in Habitat? So, it does not appear as if the minister's statement to the effect that rents in CMHC owned or controlled buildings will be frozen amounts to very much.
There is another category of project about which we have asked questions, and so far we have received, truly speaking, no direct and satisfactory answer. I am speaking of what are called limited dividend projects. In several cities of Canada, certainly in the metropolis of Toronto from where I come these days, there are a number of limited dividend projects. The residents of those limited dividend projects have received notices saying that, because their incomes have gone up, the leases which they signed in good faith will be effectively and, I am sorry to say, legally broken by the landlord because CMHC has approved increases in rents. I think we should look at these particular cases, not simply because this is a matter of concern right now in relation to increases in the old age pension, but also because the approach taken to tenants who sign leases in limited dividend projects effectively makes second class citizens of them.
When individuals in this country sign a lease with a landlord for the rental of a piece of property for a period of time, they undertake to pay a certain amount of rent and the landlord undertakes to permit them to use that property for the stated rent. It is, indeed, a rare lease in the private sector which contains a clause saying that at any given time the landlord, if his costs have gone up, may reopen that lease and stipulate another rent. This, effectively, is what is happening in many limited dividend projects in the country. Standard forms of lease are used which contain a clause which says very simply that if CMHC approval is given, the rent stipulated in the previ-
National Housing Act
ous clause will not apply and rents in the project in question can be raised.
In certain provinces of the country, certain standard forms of lease apply to people who lease in the private sector. Why should we not let the standard form of lease apply to people who live in houses that are financed by the public sector. I appeal to the minister to review those sections of the act under which such practices have been allowed, because I consider them an abuse, if not of the letter, of the spirit of the act. Surely, when we house people in limited dividend projects, and, by the way, we are not doing them any enormous favour since we are not subsidizing their rents massively, we should give them their full rights as citizens of this country. If they sign leases they should be able to live in the premises during the periods of those leases without being harassed by landlords and living under the threat that rents may go up.
I realize many members of this House know the value of a contract and the value of a lease. It is because they appreciate the value of a lease and of a contract that I wish to bring forward my next example of a matter that concerns me. In the city of Toronto, indeed, I am sure this applies to every city in this country, there are projects which are run by municipal authorities. In Toronto there is, in particular, The Metropolitan Toronto Housing Company Limited. Recently, that company has been sending out notices to its tenants advising them that, because of the increase in old age pensions, their rents will be reviewed. I should like to put on record a sample letter. Many similar copies have been sent. The one in my hand, signed by the Director of Housing, is sent from City Hall, Toronto and dated March, 1973. It reads:
Owing to announced increases in Old Age Security Pensions effective April 1, 1973, it would appear that your income may require an increase in rent, in accordance with the terms of your lease and in accordance with our agreement with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
So, at least in the view of the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Company, in accordance with the agreement it has with CMHC, it can cause a review and arrive at a decision.
For your convenience we have arranged for staff to be available in your building to take an up-to-date financial declaration on Monday, March 26th.
The staff will visit you in your apartment and I would appreciate you arranging to remain home on the above date to complete the statutory declaration.
You know, Mr. Speaker, if these people were living in standard, private housing, in no way would the landlord be able to send them a letter of this kind saying that they should stay home all day on Monday until he comes around to interview them. But, this is customary in what is, in eifect, subsidized housing. They are in effect commanded to stay around all day until the interviewers come around. I have a letter from a person who was asked to stay at home for one of these interviews. She states;
These constant interviews are terribly worrying to the people in these buildings.
I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that these instances we are speaking of involve senior citizens.

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
If we could have say a hard and fast two year lease, it would allow people to settle down with a feeling of more stability. After all, we are not going to live for another 100 years.
That is an extremely important point for anyone, but particularly for senior citizens who feel that because of the nature of the accommodation in which they find themselves they are most insecure. They are simply asking, not for a gift, but for some assurance that the contracts they enter into will be binding for a year or, as she suggests here and which I support, for a period of two years at least.
I am reminded now of another consideration of the same kind. I refer to how we approach people who live in these projects which are geared to income. I have only taken up one type of project so far. There are others which operate more directly under the provincial housing corporations. I, of course, am more familiar with what is going on in respect of the Ontario Housing Corporation. A while ago the minister said that he has not had an official reply from the minister in the province of Ontario to the letter he sent the other day asking for a freeze on rent scales. Mind you, we know there has been an unofficial answer and that Mr. Grossman said last week the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was simply playing politics with housing. It may be that Mr. Grossman knows whereof he speaks, but at any rate he gave an answer which indicates that the OHC had not raised rents and did not even do so the last time there was an increase in old age pensions. It is an interesting shell game we have going on here.
There is in Sault Ste. Marie, for example, an authority called the Sault Ste. Marie Housing Authority which has been sending out notices of rent increases to old age pensioners because their pensions have been increased. We could say this is a project of a limited dividend nature and they are therefore operating under section 15 of the National Housing Act. However, if we look a little further we find that the people in this project who complain about rent increases receive letters from the Ontario Housing Corporation to this effect:
I aknowledge and thank you for your letter of February 3, 1973 concerning the increase in your monthly rent. I have investigated this matter with the Sault Ste. Marie Housing Authority and I find that they have acted in accordance with the procedures set in the provincial rent scale and your rent was computed directly as stated. However, if you are still in doubt I suggest that you contact the manager of the Sault Ste. Marie Housing Authority who will I am sure explain in detail how he arrives at the increase.
This letter is signed by the area manager of the Northern Branch of the Ontario Housing Corporation. So, what exactly is happening here? It is all very well for the minister to say, as if he were reporting a fiat, that we at the federal level have commanded that there shall be no rent increases in CMHC controlled or owned buildings, but in effect this amounts to nothing. It is all very well for the minister to say that he has written to all provincial ministers asking them to freeze all rent scales, but even when the rent scales are frozen people are still being forced to go up within the scales. We have announcements from the various provincial ministers to the effect that the minister at the federal level does not know what he is talking about because their authorities have not increased rents and yet, on the other hand, we have evidence that

various aspects of these housing authorities have increased rents.
I understand that some of the municipal housing authorities are, in effect, providing housing subsidies, which bring up another problem. If they do not increase rents their costs go up and, in effect, they will be handing out more subsidies to their tenants because rents will remain at the same level. I have more correspondence from another municipal authority. This is from the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority. It is a letter to one of the Toronto aldermen explaining why there must be an increase in rents. The letter reads:
What is essential to remember, however, is that the geared-to-income basis is part of a formal agreement with CMHC which requires us to make these adjustments.
Note the words, "which requires us to make these adjustments".
We would, therefore, be reporting to the Board of Directors on the consequences of the action which we will take and I would assume the information provided to the Board of Directors would also come to the Social Services and Housing Committee.
The important part of this communication is that this authority, the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority, feels required under the agreements they have with CMHC to make these upward adjustments. It would be appreciated if, first of all, in his response to the very important points made in this House in respect of these amendments to the National Housing Act the minsiter would make a full and complete statement concerning the impact and significance of his interventions on behalf of the senior citizens of this country, interventions which we were led to believe were made about some kind of control and freeze on rents. Secondly, I wonder whether the minister would be willing to countenance further amendments to the act which would clear up the intent of the act, this preventing this kind of abuse because there is no question that there are abuses.
I cite again for his consideration the example of the limited dividend projects which are very faintly subsidized by the public. Hon. members know that the rents in limited dividend projects are not much less than the rents in the private market place. Because of the fact the government has a few dollars involved in this, we insist that these tenants not be treated as second-class citizens. They should have a lease which would give them security for a year or for two years. Surely we can review this aspect of the act and write into it language which will prevent this kind of abuse and distortion.
Third, if the minister is serious about having a rent freeze in respect of projects for which there already exist formal binding agreements between CMHC and the various housing authorities at the municipal level in this country, then he must also be prepared to help in respect of the kind of burden that is involved in the added subsidy. I am sure it will be possible for the minister, under section 44 of the Act, to make funds available under the NHA to compensate the various housing authorities for the increased subsidy these authorities will have to pay if they are to comply with the request of the minister not to increase rents. In my case, I would like to see the Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority compensated.
March 21, 1973

I would like to conclude my remarks by simply reiterating my appeal, first of all, for a full and complete statement of what the effects of the various requests made of the minister with regard to freezing rents would be so that we can get a complete picture of exactly what this involves. When we are told that CMHC has fixed the rents of Habitat in Montreal, in effect, we are being told that virtually nothing has been done for the senior citizens in this country. Second, I will repeat my appeal to look at those aspects of the act under which certain abuses, particularly to senior citizens, have been caused in this country.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate on Bill C-133 which puts forward the government's panacea to Canada's housing problems. In fairness, I suppose, I should really call this bill a partial panacea because the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) has said that this bill is just part of some sort of vast, comprehensive plan which, he implies, will end Canada's housing problems once and for all. I for one, and I am sure all Canadians, would like to see this plan and would like to have the minister present this blueprint for urban bliss, or even some tangible evidence that such a blueprint exists because, on the evidence so far available, I think there is good reason to be highly sceptical that such a blueprint or such a plan exists.
Certainly, this bill before us gives me no confidence that its sponsors are aware of the root problems which are causing millions of Canadians to continue to live in less than adequate housing, and certainly there is no evidence that this bill's sponsors have developed a surefire plan, a strategy, let alone some legislation which, when implemented, will ensure that every Canadian, if he desires, will be able, at some time in his life, to purchase a home with a landscape and with room to live, not just to exist or just to sleep and eat. One does not have to be a trained social scientist nor even particularly observant, to see the effects upon an individual or a family of being forced to live in housing which provides just shelter and nothing else.
In my constituency of Calgary Centre, which consists of the central core of a large and rapidly growing urban centre, there are unfortunately thousands of examples of the tragic situation which I am convinced results from improper housing, among other things. It is obvious to me that every social problem conceivable, from alcoholism to child beating and from family breakdown to juvenile delinquency, is exacerbated by improper housing. Here, I include all the factors such as living space, open land, noise, traffic, dirt and population density. That is why my party and I consider the area of housing and urban affairs to be of paramount importance, and that is why we are so dissappointed in this bill.
My colleague, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has accurately described this bill as a "band-aid bill". It will provide some comfort in some areas, and therefore we will support it, but it will not cure the problem any more than a bandaid will cure internal injury or disease. What we have in this bill is a continuation of the
National Housing Act
practice of this government over far too many years of proposing ad hoc solutions to treat problems affecting a complex system, but perceived by the government as isolated, independent problems.
In September of 1971 the Science Council of Canada published its fourteenth report entitled "Cities for Tomorrow" in which they make several, I believe nine in all, recommendations for ways in which the federal government can make our cities more liveable for people. But the fundamental point made by this report, which the government does not seem to appreciate, is that the city is a system or, in simpler terms, everything relates to everything else. It is on this basis that my colleagues and I form our main criticism of this bill, and indeed of this government.
The problems of housing and of urban affairs must be considered simultaneously, in concert with each other, for they are all part of a system and require a system's approach or, as my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) stated, a massive approach on all sectors of the problems. The ad hoc or bandaid approach in this bill, though completely consistent with the ad hoc approaches of this government to all of our important national problems, will unfortunately not cure Canada's housing problems and, in fact, will not even significantly alter the continuing trend under this Trudeau government of deteriorating housing situations in Canada, let alone alter the deteriorating urban problems in general. With each passing day more and more Canadians are removed from the ranks of those who can afford a house of their own. This bill will not alter that trend significantly. That is the tragedy of this bill and, indeed, of this government. The young people in my riding and throughout Canada will continue to be disappointed and will have to wait that much longer before the Stanfield government takes office and cures this deplorable situation. They have, amongst others, the NDP to thank for that delay.
The main problem in housing today is that costs have risen to such a degree that very few people can afford to buy their own houses. On a national average, less than 10 per cent of Canadian families can afford to buy an NHA home. That compares to nearly 50 per rent 12 years ago. That is the fundamental problem, and this bill will not help.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Neither will the Tories.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In fact, the only portion of this bill that really directs itself toward this fundamental problem is that pertaining to land banking. However, I am afraid this scheme, which is intended to reduce the cost of land, will not have that effect and indeed, in the short term, will probably have the opposite effect. After all, you do not have to be an expert to realize that the introduction of a large scale buyer into an already restricted or short-supply market is bound to increase prices, not decrease them. Perhaps in 10 years municipal governments will be in a position to reduce speculative land increase by releasing publicly held lands for residential dwellings, but in the meantime land prices will continue to skyrocket.
What is needed is great increases in the supply of serviced land, which really means massive increases in servicing. This bill does not provide the municipalities with

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
the inducement or means to construct the large scale transportation and service corridors that are necessary. Raw land is expensive because serviced land is expensive, and serviced land is expensive because developers must build all the roads, services, etc. for their development, plus provide the capacity to handle developments that will take place farther out. Developers must pay for these services because municipalities lack the resources or tax base to put them in themselves. That indicates what the thrust should be to truly reduce land costs now, not some time in the future.
We should supply the funds or help the municipalities through low interest loans to service large tracts of raw land. That will reduce the price of residential lots and of raw land. That will help Canadians buy a house of their own. It will reduce the cost of housing in general now, not some ten years in the future. But the rising cost of land is not the only factor which is causing house prices to rise at the rate they are. In fact, I am not sure it is the main factor. Based on my observations and my discussions with home builders and home buyers, the most expensive aspect of buying a home today is the cost of mortgage money. Since the Trudeau government took office, the cost of mortgage money has risen from less than 7 per cent to more than 9 per cent. As my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe pointed out, since 1961 the cost of the average house has almost doubled, but when you add financing charges, the cost has almost tripled.
This problem, which is clearly the most important item or cause of increased housing costs, is not even alluded to in this bill. You would think the minister might at least have provided a bandaid for this sore if he lacks the wherewithal to devise a cure. Perhaps it is time that long-term mortgage capital was removed from the general money market manipulations so that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Bank of Canada can no longer use these interest rates in their inane attempts to cure inflation, recession, or whatever. Most countries of the world do a far better job than Canada in arranging for a ready supply of reasonably priced mortgages for the housing markets.
We, in Canada, not only do nothing to ensure a stable supply of low cost mortgage funds, but in fact use this money supply, and the housing and construction sector in general, as the main tool in accelerating and decelerating the economy. This has led to a very fragmented and inefficient housing industry. Many of the home builders in Calgary are just now recovering from the Trudeau government's tight money policy, that is, those who survived at all. And those who did survive are very apprehensive and concerned about what other inane moves the government might make, and thus are protecting themselves in a way that is itself causing increased housing costs. Who can blame them? With this government in charge no one can be faulted for not being willing to invest heavily in developing extensive land holdings. A large inventory of serviced lots is not an asset in a tight money situation.
That, Sir, is the essence of the measures the government should be introducing to reduce housing costs. It should be working to reduce the interest on mortgage loans, and to remove mortgage financing from the "boom or bust"

manipulations of the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.
Another factor which is a major contributor to the high cost of urban housing, is municipal taxes and municipal financing. There is nothing in this bill, nor in any announced government program, that addresses itself to this problem. Most people, when considering the purchase of a new home are, from a financial point of view, interested in two things, the down payment and the monthly payments, consisting of principal, interest and taxes. The payment on the principal is usually trivial in comparison with the other two. With 80 per cent of our population soon to be dwelling in a few urban centres, it is clear that the responsibilities and financial obligations of the cities will not be decreasing. They require, and will continue to require large amounts of money. If their main source is to remain the revenue that comes from property tax, then these taxes will remain high, and will remain a significant obstacle to home ownership for millions of Canadians.
Notwithstanding constitutional considerations, there are lots of things the federal government could have considered doing to help in this area as well. Here again, we might have expected the government at least to offer a bandaid, or some small relief, if not a cure.
There is of course another very significant factor in the cost of housing which neither the bill nor the government has considered. I refer to the increased cost in building the house itself. Granted that these increased costs may be tied in an integral way to the whole inflationary spiral, with which this inept tragedy of a government has been struggling unsuccessfully for too long, but there are things which could have been done to reduce housing costs. If the Minister of Urban Affairs is truly concerned about the cost of housing, why did he not prevail on his colleague, the Minister of Finance, to adopt even more of the Progressive Conservative platform and remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials?
If the government was genuinely committed to a policy of good and proper housing for all Canadians, it would have removed this 11 per cent sales tax. A Stanfield government will remove this tax, because a Stanfield government will be committed to a policy of providing Canadians with the opportunity to own their own homes, with a yard, with some room to live, and a neighbourhood that is liveable. We are committed to providing housing at reasonable cost for all Canadians.
I do not think the government holds these types of objectives in very high esteem, and certainly not this minister. On March 6, 1973, I asked the minister whether his department was aware of and was investigating the tremendous increases that are occurring in the cost of lumber, in some cases by as much as 100 per cent in the last year. He referred me to the Minister of Finance. I would think that a minister responsible for housing at least would be aware of the factors or elements contributing to the tremendous increase in housing costs.
There is nothing in this bill, nor in any government policies or actions that could lead one to believe that they will reduce the cost of housing, or even abate the present trends. As I have indicated, the main factors in the increased housing costs are interest rates, shortage of serviced land, municipal taxes, federal taxes and fiscal
March 21, 1973

policies, and building construction and material costs. This bill only addresses itself to one of these factors, and in a way that will have marginal, if any, beneficial effect, and none in the short term.
In the time I have left, I want to mention briefly some other aspects of the bill. By and large these are good measures, although I repeat they are no panacea for the problems they purport to cure. I am especially pleased that the government has decided to support the restoration rather than destruction of old neighbourhoods. Many of the neighbourhoods in my constituency could use this type of assistance. Certainly, the people living there would welcome the relief of no longer having to fear the bulldozer. Too often in the past people living in older neighbourhoods, many of whom have raised their families there, and who wanted to spend the remainder of their lives there, were disregarded, or forcibly moved, or had to witness the destruction of their familiar surroundings under the guise of progress or urban renewal. I hope that these items in the bill reflect a sincere change of heart on the part of the government, and that we can now consider the restoration of neighbourhoods and of houses as the most desirable form of renewal.
On Monday night my colleague, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey), directed most of his speech toward this aspect of Bill C-133, and I will not repeat the reasoned arguments he presented, except to re-emphasize the dangers of excessive centralization in the administration of this bill. I hope the minister will consider this point most carefully, since it may well determine the degree to which items like this in the bill have or do not have the desired beneficial consequences.
I would like also to state that the increased protection for home buyers is a welcome item, although it should be extended to more than just NHA secured mortgages. It is my understanding that since private mortgage insuring companies have entered this market, the percentage of NHA insured mortgages has decreased significantly, so much so that CMHC is now considerably over-staffed. Perhaps that is another reason we have not been able to get the CMHC annual report! However, the main point, as it relates to this legislation, is that the majority of new homes will not be covered.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the question of research and development, this item was one of the recommendations in the Science Council's report to which I referred earlier. I am glad to see that this recommendation at least was adopted. Certainly, when considering the technological advances in almost every facet of our society, it can be seen that housing has lagged far behind.
I would like to make one suggestion as to how this item might be further improved. One of the main reasons technological innovation as it pertains to housing has lagged behind other fields is a reflection of the fragmented nature of the housing and construction industries. This fragmentation is due in large part to government policies. However, be that as it may, true technological innovation is enhanced by encouraging experimentation over a broad front, by many people in many areas, and small, or even moderate sized builders lack the base to do much research. They simply cannot afford to take the risk. However, they do generate new ideas, come in contact
National Housing Act
with new materials and new techniques. There would be far greater utilization of this new technology if the risks could be shared. That is why I would suggest the government might consider an insurance scheme to insure innovative or novel new techniques, and/or materials, and thereby reduce the risk factor. This would greatly broaden the experimental base and lead ultimately to greater progress in developing newer, better and cheaper housing.
In conclusion, may I say that I will support this bill even though it is no panacea for our housing problems. It will not reduce housing costs. It will not cure Canada's housing problems. However, hopefully it will do more good than harm. My main fear is that it may cause the government to be content, thinking it has addressed itself to the real housing problems of Canada, and thus delay the true changes that are necessary. However, this concern is quickly ameliorated when I realize that what we are dealing with is a temporary government which will soon be replaced by a Stanfield government-

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, aside from the whole question of unemployment, rising prices and the other domestic and international economic matters that face us, this government, and the government from our party that will follow it, face their greatest challenge in this country in the field of urban affairs. The shortage and inadequacy of urban housing, traffic and transportation problems, air and water pollution, the conflicting jungle of land use and decaying neighbourhoods, urban poverty, social disturbance and the frustrations of municipal administrators are familiar problems to the average Canadian city dweller today. In that litany of urban tragedy, Mr. Speaker, lies the challenge facing all the governments of Canada. There is a general consensus that the problems of urban society have multiplied and intensified so greatly that they endanger, and indeed threaten, the long term vitality of the cities as we know them.
The present methods of dealing with these problems have been judged inadequate by even impartial advisers and comprehensive new approaches have been advocated. I say to this House and to you, Mr. Speaker, that this government has not listened. That is not to say that Bill C-133 is not an improvement on the situation because obviously it is, but in terms of a comprehensive, national urban policy it is not; it falls far short of that category.
The problem, Mr. Speaker, has not been the lack of research, but an apparent unwillingness to make comprehensive decisions and to finance national goals for urban Canada. It is true that for the majority of people the large metropolitan areas are becoming less desirable each year. That includes the area that abuts my own constituency,

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
this city, which is becoming less desirable because of transportation problems. The failure of this government to meet the financial requirements of the regional transit commission quickly, and to develop rapid surface transit within this city, has caused a type of urban decay which is becoming more discernible each day and each month because the action that is required and that members of this House have called for has not been taken.
I do not think it falls upon us in this country to compare ourselves with other places in North America. We have heard the classic comparisons with New York, San Francisco and Chicago and the conclusion that we are not as bad as they are, thank God. With continued neglect and continuing inability to meet real needs, with continued frustration in the whole governmental process, with the wrangling over legislative responsibility, whether it is provincial, municipal or federal, we run the risk in some of our cities, and I believe this is one, of passing the point where anything can be accomplished quickly to improve the quality of life.
The statistical hallmarks of the problems that face us, face this government and will face succeeding governments if action is not taken, are rather frightening. In 1921, less than half our population was urban; by 1966, the proportion was 73 per cent; by 1981, it is expected to reach 85 per cent and in the year 2000 it is projected to rise to 94 per cent. By the year 2000, Mr. Speaker, nine out of every ten Canadians in Quebec, Ontario, the Maritimes, Alberta and British Columbia are expected to be living in the cities and towns. Within 30 years it is expected that more than 50 per cent of Canada's population, some 16 million people, will reside in 21 centres stretching along the St. Lawrence lowlands from Windsor to Quebec City. Mr. Speaker, in light of those statistical hallmarks of the urban problem, we in Canada have no cause for any self-righteous smugness. It is a fact that for many reasons people are leaving rural Canada and are crowding into our cities. This input of people is complicating the problem of urban renewal every day and is making the decision in large cities on urban renewal, low rental housing, senior citizens' housing, and many other fields, the decision that is born out of desperation and pressure rather than reasoned consideration.
Is it not obvious that the availability of serviced land is an important and indeed fundamental need in all our cities? It is so obvious that it hardly bears repeating. It is also obvious that there has been a failure, wherever the blame lies in this country, to provide an adequate supply of serviced land. That, too, hardly bears repeating. The story is contained in the excellent speeches of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) and the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) who spoke before me.
I think it is a wrong concept in every part of our lives, Mr. Speaker, that it has become fashionable to be bigger, as if bigness had some sort of grace attached to it-to have more and to do it all for less. I realize that this ministry or this government cannot stop the clock and it is foolish to say that of any government, but in this country we have the opportunity now to change the pattern of our cities and, I suggest to change the direction of our growth.

However, I do not in any way minimize the size of the task that faces any government which wishes to face up to it. We have an opportunity to do something in Canada before it is too late. This will require the co-ordinated recognition of the problem by all levels of government; it will require the leadership of the federal government, not just in money but in ideas and in courage. This bill does not contain these kinds of ideas or the courage that is required.
We have to fight what I call the inevitability syndrome in Canada. People say it is inevitable that Toronto will have a population of six million people by the year 2000; it is inevitable that cities will be filled only with high rise buildings and there will be no room for houses and families. They say it is inevitable that we will have urban sprawl. Mr. Speaker, I suggest these things are not inevitable, and whether they happen depends upon the actions of government backed by an awakening people in these communities that are fighting this pinch in the manner I have suggested.
Our big fight against this inevitability syndrome in urban affairs is the concept of new communities mentioned in this bill and the extension of older communities. Those are older communities divorced from the areas of difficulty that I have described. Perhaps it may prove the most significant part of this bill in terms of its long range impact on the future development of our country.
The new provisions in Bill C-133 are contained in clauses 45.1, 45.2 and 45.3. If these clauses are administered and funded with the leadership and courage that we would expect of a government, but which we have not seen since January 4, 1973, and if there is proper consultation with the provincial governments, particularly those where there is a real urban problem, we can start to acquire or provide for the acquisition of land for new communities. The bill provides for this and it provides for the acquisition of land for transportation corridors, for open space and for essential public facilities. I think the cost-sharing arrangements in the bill are generous; they indicate that Central Mortgage and Housing will share 75 per cent of the cost as well as 75 per cent of the profits or losses.
My suggestion to the minister, Mr. Speaker, is that the new communities program should not be restricted solely to areas removed from existing cities and towns. As I read the clause, it could provide for the incorporation of the development of new communities within urban areas, as well as the development around the cities of extensions to existing communities. In this way, I believe it would be possible in new communities to have not merely dormitories, but mixed urban areas in which the commercial and industrial amenities which are necessary to life, work and function, as well as the assessment based for municipalities, would be present and where there would be at the time of the development around these towns the existing social structure to support them. This social structure would be augmented by these new communities.
If there is an ultimate feeling, it is that a beneficial housing policy cannot be developed in isolation from other programs. Perhaps this is the failing in this bill. The
March 21, 1973

government still has no strategy for urban growth. There is no strategy with regard to rapid transit or the provision in municipalities of other transportation facilities. There is an ad hoc approach to the whole problem of servicing. The bill does not present any specific outline for such a policy with respect to the very excellent program it sets forth for the development of new communities. It shirks the issue by speaking vaguely of transportation corridors.
I have one other matter to which I should like to refer, and that is the whole question of senior citizens' housing. I am going to relate this matter to the whole problem which affects the province of Ontario, particularly eastern Ontario. In eastern Ontario, the populations of many small towns and villages were growing up until 10 years ago. In that area of Ontario, we are now feeling this urban movement of population. As a result, in many small villages and towns in eastern Ontario there is an aging of the population. As this aging process occurs, there is a greater and greater requirement for continuing provision of adequate senior citizens' housing. That is a need.
I have two matters in my constituency in mind. There has never, and will not be in the foresseable future, municipal services of sewer and water to supply not only senior citizens' accommodation but single family accommodation, commercial and other development that takes place. I think a wrong policy has developed at Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which reports to this parliament through the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. It seems the policy of that corporation is that there shall be none of these multiple unit projects such as senior citizens' developments until there is a system of municipal sewer and water services. This is very important because we are not going to be able to fulfil a need for these aging populations. I have a case in point.
I wrote to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with regard to a senior citizens' project for the townships of Marlborough and North Gower in my constituency. I also have in mind one in the village of Spencerville which is a police village, a small hamlet. I have not heard from CMHC with regard to the one matter, but I have heard with regard to the proposal in the township of North Gower. In my letter, I asked what was the general policy and whether it was required to have sewer and water when considering multiple units for senior citizens. I received a reply from CMHC dated March 2, 1973, and I quote:
The absence of municipal sewer and water services could present a real problem inasmuch as it has been Corporation policy for some years now that financing would not be made available for the construction of "multiple-unit" projects in locations not served by piped sewers. This policy reflects our concern with the growing problem of soil and water pollution created in part by the use of septic tanks.
I cannot quarrel with the minister's concern about pollution control. It is a concern of us all. I concede that there is always the possibility of improperly installed or operating septic tanks causing difficulty. However, this lack should not become the basis for automatic rejection of projects. With all the research facilities available in this country, this ministry should be the leader in establishing research projects to develop sewage disposal systems that are not dependent upon the septic system, but can operate in isolation from municipal sewer and water systems.

this work as well. There has to be a spirit of co-operation such as is now beginning in the partnership between the senior citizens and CMHC. This has to be extended to all forms of housing and servicing of land.
It is all very well to blame the land developer for making a dollar. We should remember that it is the policies of the government with respect to its housing program which have enabled the land developer to make his profits. The shortage of housing is the result of the failure of the federal government to show initiative. To this day, the government has failed to present a national urban development policy.
