speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the real reason we were quarrelling over the location of the minister's residence was a natural inquiry by the members of my party as to how many times he and his colleagues have voted.
I want to open my remarks today with some reference to the remarks of the minister when he began this debate, particularly the piety that he exhibited at that time and before when he stated that "good housing at reasonable cost is the social right of every citizen of this country". When good housing at reasonable cost is not available, the minister has been quite adept at finding excuses, usually blaming some other level of government. However, it is my privilege to represent in this House three of the town-sites in national parks and in those townsites the housing crisis is a scandal, as it has been for years. They are areas completely within the jurisdiction of the federal government. This is a crisis which is completely the fault of the federal government. When I asked the minister in this House the other day whether that pious principle of his applied to areas within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government, he ducked the question, passing it on to a minister who was not here.
What is important is that the housing crisis which exists in areas within federal jurisdiction does not apply just to national parks and townsites there. It is the shocking fact that the people in Canada whose needs in housing are most acute and least recognized are those who dwell within the exclusive domain of the federal government. I refer to the people trapped in the colonial tentacles of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, native people, northern people and residents of
March 21, 1973

national parks. If the minister is serious in his assertion about a social right to good housing at reasonable cost for every citizen, he presumably regards these Canadians as second class citizens.
These areas are directly within federal jurisdiction and, at least in so far as the parks are concerned, the minister should either reform the practices of his colleagues or refrain from pious declarations of empty principle. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development once told residents of Jasper that if they did not like it there they could leave. He is now making that necessary; they have no houses in which to live. Newspapers in that town are now running advertisements for apartments in adjoining communities because you cannot get any place to live in communities that are administered exclusively by the federal government. The problem will be much more critical this summer with the influx of students and tourists, and despite the repeated assurances of the minister as to the social right of Canadians, the federal government is proposing to do nothing about the situation.
The second reference that I want to make to the minister's statement is drawn from his reference on page 2258 of Hansard to this bill being only part of the total picture. It is quite significant that the minister finds he has to start his contribution to this debate with an apology. As my colleagues have already said in this debate, the major fault with this legislation and with the entire approach to policy of this minister, is that it is an ad hoc approach. Even now we have had no sign of a genuine national policy. I suggest it is misleading to suggest that this is part of a picture, because no picture exists. We have a piecemeal approach. Some of the pieces are good. But we cannot delay much longer the development of an over-all policy. We have to recognize that what we are dealing with here is not just housing policy; we are dealing with social, cultural and economic policy. We are dealing with the people of the country as a whole.
All these matters are inter-related. That was supposed to have been recognized when the Department of Urban Affairs was established, but that mandate has been abandoned. There is now an obvious and continuing conflict between CMHC and the minister's own cadre of advisers. There is no agreement between them as to jurisdiction or as to goals. The minister himself is either unable or unwilling to resolve this conflict and to give any kind of leadership.
We need in Canada an over-all strategy which recognizes the relationship between various aspects of national policy, which treats housing as being not in isolation from the rest of the problems of the country; which treats the CMHC as being not in isolation from the goals or other aspects of the Department of Urban Affairs. What we will be doing in this area will affect the face and the future of the country forever.
We will have to have much more co-ordination than has been the case to date because what we are doing now is stumbling in the dark without goals, without agreement on how to reach goals, with a minister who claims that a major piece of legislation is really only part of a picture, but who admits by his every action and inaction that it is a picture he cannot see, let alone achieve.
National Housing Act
I have some sympathy for the minister. He is up against the established practice of treating housing and other policies as though they were in some vacuum. He symbolizes indeed the plight of a party which is listening to advisers and following procedures which are decades out of date. Perhaps the most critical issue in this country is the fact that one party and one group of advisers have been running Canada for most of the last 40 years. The senior advisers did their best during the Diefenbaker administration to frustrate reforms intended and initiated there. They are running the country now in a way that, however appropriate to the 30's or the 40's or the 50's, is dangerously wrong in contemporary Canada.
I want to focus on one feature of this bill. It is a feature referred to by my colleague from Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) as the new communities provision. I am concerned, as he is, that there is not adequate provision in that proposal for application to existing communities. I think that the new communities proposal is a symbol of a policy that, while it might be good on its own, should not stand on its own, and indeed which holds the promise of doing harm precisely because it does stand alone and is not part of an integrated policy towards communities in Canada.
The purposes of that section are self-evident and good. They are going to relieve congestion. They are going to allow experimentation and might even help open resource areas. But by my reading the provision applies only to wholly new communities and things created where nothing was before-the product exclusively of social engineering. There is no provision for expansion around communities that already exist, which have already proven that they are places where people want to live. Perhaps my reading is wrong; perhaps the bill does not preclude that possibility, although to the degree the new communities concept relies upon the instrument of land assembly the concept would seem to preclude additions to towns and small communities that already exist. But even if that possibility does exist, it will obviously be as an afterthought, as an adjunct to the prior purpose of creating wholly new, experimental, engineered communities.
There are a lot of things that are not in this bill. To my mind, coming from where I do, the most serious absence is the absence of any policy at all to develop or to maintain the thousands of towns and small communities which, if they survive, hold the promise of giving modern Canada a style and quality of life without parallel in any other country in the world. I want to suggest that in housing and in other policies, this government has sentenced to death several of the smaller and older communities in Canada which have a lot of natural life left in them if they are given an even break through national policy.
Throughout his long address the other day, the minister devoted fully two sentences to what he called "the deeply satisfying aspects of life in the country and in country towns and villages". He talked about their contribution to what his speechwriters called "the abiding values that have made Canada and her people great". Those words reek of eulogy. The minister and his aides clearly regard these smaller communities as a part of the past-albeit the abiding past-and he pauses in his blind rush towards a future he admits he cannot see only long enough to wish

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
these country towns and villages a decent burial. The minister might deny that. He might claim that he has plans, that this is all part of that elusive, larger picture. But the damage is done by his demonstrated indifference.
My grandfather ran a newspaper in southwestern Alberta in a day and a district where you could not always phone to check your facts. In one issue he reported the death of a merchant in the little town of Longview, a man called Long Tom. The obituary was properly full of praise and respect. The day after the paper appeared so did Long Tom, who said the reports of his death were premature, and while he appreciated all the nice things that had been said, they were certainly hurting business. That is precisely the situation of the smaller communities of Canada. They can appreciate the lofty language of the minister but know that, in the cadence of his words and the thrust of his policy is the sound of a death knell that is not only premature but destructive of the values and the future of this country. The minister can say what he will, but his policies are hurting the business and hurting the life of the smaller communities of Canada.
May I give one small example? The federal funding that will go into these new communities will give them an unfair competitive advantage over neighbourhood communities that already exist and have to get along with the infusion of federal funds and expertise. Indeed, under this bill the only help, potentially, that will be given to existing communities, as I see it, is provided for in the hinterland housing proposal, and that is far too limited.
The problem, Sir, is not so much in what the bill does as in what it fails to do. In fact, in Canada there has been for a long time discrimination against small communities. It is not deliberate. I suggest that they are simply the so-called accidental victims of policies established for other purposes. They are too small and too unorganized to defend themselves against the cumulative, contrary resources of big governments, big cities, big labour and big industry. They are the communities that are overlooked. We see it in housing policy.
The minister talks about housing surveys. Actually, CMHC has made virtually no surveys outside major metropolitan areas. He talks of regional surveys. Regional programs might be planned, but they have not happened. The focus has been on one, two or three of our major cities. As well, most towns in Canada suffer from the so-called red circle policy of CMHC which limits and virtually eliminates CMHC lending in areas which are not considered economically viable and which are slung into that category without any effective power of appeal. This might not be official policy, but it is effective policy. It is discrimination against smaller places which, to a certain mentality, are not viable because they are not big.
Most serious, Sir, is the fact that the department is simply and blindly going along with trends, responding to projections which might very well be wrong and working without targets, without goals, which might recognize and value the strength of smaller places. Instead of targets being aimed at, there is a simple an unquestioning capitulation to figures which show people are moving to metropolitan areas; and there is not any attempt to determine
(Mr. Clark (Rocky Mountain).)
whether they need to or want to move in such numbers. There is a danger, Sir, when making the kind of case I am trying to make today, of being accused of retreating to nostalgia and attempting to maintain artificially communities which time has passed by. That is too easy a response. I appreciate, as all members of the House do, the tremendous importance of urban growth in this country. I appreciate particularly the capacity of our larger cities to provide innovation and excitement in our national fabric. We value such cities. We welcome them. We want them to be as good and as strong as possible. Obviously, there are places in Canada that were thriving once and are empty now. Of course, the place to remember our legitimate rural past is Upper Canada Village, or Heritage Park, or the local museum, or in personal memories that one finds across the country. But, Sir, to say that some small communities will die is not at all the same as saying that all small communities must die. There is too much evidence that the latter assumption guides this government and its advisers, the assumption that the small community, in all its forms, is doomed and that our future lies exclusively in bigger and bigger cities.
I ask you, Sir, to consider what has been happening in Canada. We have a national policy whose purpose is, according to the government, to rationalize small farms; that is a fancy word which means putting them out of business. We have a national policy which acquiesces in rail-line abandonment and thus cuts the cord which might give smaller places the same chance to live that larger places have. It is interesting to note, parenthetically, that when a major change is planned in the transportation patterns serving larger centres, there is immediately something called an impact study. But when a railway proposes to tear up service to a town and do damage far greater in proportion than an airport at Pickering would, we accept the system of Canadian Transport Commission hearings, where corporate experts consistently prevail over the innocent or unsophisticated arguments of small town mayors or reeves.
We have a national industrial policy which continues to concentrate secondary industrial development in a handful of crowded places, even though technology and economics would allow much greater decentralization. We had a national budget brought down last month which will have the effect of drying up even more the moneys available to provinces, which means that when the provinces split their smaller pies the towns and villages which have none of the expertise which cities can hire will suffer disproportionately. Even the National Youth Orchestra, Mr. Speaker, draws disproportionately from larger centres and leaves too many of the children of the towns and villages with their talents untested.
Any one of us privileged to serve an area of towns and smaller places can cite a hundred other instances of unintended discrimination, a hundred other instances of the assumption that the small community is doomed. None of us alleges a conspiracy. No one is out to get the town or village. They are simply being overlooked, and when they raise their voice in protest or proposal, they are too easily dismissed by commentators and public servants to whom the towns went out with Stephen Leacock and whose only picture of the country now is of some cracker-barrel caricature mopping up after Charlotte Gobeil.
March 21, 1973

Two things are happening. First, we have artificially defined the future, and done so by accident without any real inquiry or research. We do not know that we want massive cities; we simply assume we will have them and shape our policy to achieve our prophecy. The second thing that is happening is simply that national policy is being devised to meet other needs which have more urgent advocates. Too often smaller places suffer as a side effect. Some people assume that the only way to maintain viable smaller communities is by some artificial act, some interference with the natural processes of growth, whatever they are. In fact, the threat to towns and small communities is precisely that the acts of interference or artifice which governments create or condone have been biased against the smaller community. For example, the interference implicit in the new communities provisions of this bill will mean that existing small communities will now face new federally funded competitors for industry and population. The towns do not rely on artifice; they are its victims. The interfering has already been done against the interests of the smaller places and what is needed now is not a special concession but an even break.
I want to return to the question of forecasting, to the prophecies of extravagant urban growth and the actions and assumptions which can make those prophecies selffulfilling. When Professor Lithwick submitted his report on urban Canada in December 1970, he included a projection that some 73 per cent of Canada's population will live in 12 major cities by the year 2001. There were similar projections painting a similar future and implying the withering away of smaller places. Professor Lithwick is no longer with the government. It is my impression that one of the reasons is that, while he submitted those projections as a warning of what could happen, the government took them as a goal for what should happen. Public servants and private planners took note of the statistics, chewed them over coffee, agreed that indeed cities did seem to be growing and so a sort of unconscious consensus was formed; and every bureaucrat, every businessman and every student planning a career shapes his or her plans in the context of that vision of the future. The question we should be asking as the parliament of all of Canada, as the custodian of the nation's history and quality of life, is whether that is the vision we want to achieve, whether we want a Canada with only 12 major centres or whether we want a country with more balance and variety.
The tragedy of this bill, Sir, and of this government is that those questions are not even being asked. Perhaps there is come cubbyhole in CMHC or in the minister's own private zoo where people are paid to wonder about the future. But it does not show in the bill, it does not show in policy on transportation, as my colleague the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) said yesterday, and it does not show in policy on finance or on industrial development. All that shows, instead, is a more or less mindless acceptance of an untested trend.
I am not going to go on at length to celebrate the virtues of small communities. As the minister said in his little eulogy, they are abiding virtues. In fact, we have in the literature and lore of Canada a rural tradition of uncommon strength and influence. Even now, our poets, writers
National Housing Act
and singers invoke the language of the land when they want to speak to Canadians. But apart from that tradition, apart from our unusual history of settlement and growth in a network of smaller places, apart even from the desire of so many Canadians to go back to smaller places for a weekend or a vacation or, if they can afford it, for a "home in the country", this parliament should consider that the very virtues we seek to achieve by legislation have grown by habit in most of the towns and villages of our countryside.
We try to contrive in cities a sense of neighbourhood; yet that exists in towns. We try to inspire a respect for environment; yet, no one raised, for example, in a prairie town could escape a sense of the wonder and the frailty of nature. We are worried about rootlessness and anomie, yet there are abundant communities in Canada that are still places where people feel at home, where democracy is genuinely participatory, where neighbours are known. Of course, these places have limitations of their own and should be assessed as critically as cities are. The point is that Canada in the 1970's has the chance to draw the best from both the town tradition and the urban fact. Perhaps no other country in the world shares that opportunity. Others have squandered their rural resources, or are necessarily preoccupied with establishing the elements of an urban society. We still have time to strike a balance and, perhaps in so doing we can help define the elusive Canadian identity and develop communities which meet modern human needs. But it will not happen by accident. It will not happen as a result of bills like this, which simply ignore the rich resource we have in the towns and small communities of Canada. And it will not happen unless this government or its replacement, turns around the present attitude toward smaller communities.
The question of small communities is only part of the problem or, as the minister would say, only part of the picture we face in this debate when we deal with this problem. Before we begin to be satisfied that we have a national urban policy or, as I would prefer to call it, a national community policy, we must recognize the danger of a piecemeal approach. Not only does this measure fail to do things we need to have done, but can, as in the case of towns, cause positive harm. We require an integrated policy which recognizes that the goals of different sectors of our society must be set together and sought together, and which recognizes that what we do in transportation and industrial development affects our housing policy. We must remember that what we do to build up cities can cause smaller communities to die.
My own preoccupation today is with towns, and similar smaller communities. That is for two reasons. First, they possess a unique set of values which, if encouraged, can enrich the nation. Second, their plight today, the danger they face, is due to the neglect of national policies, more than to any other factor. Unlike other groups they have few people to present their case.
This bill fails even to recognize the importance of towns. The minister, or his apologists, might say that the provisions concerning consultation allow provinces to establish priorities for towns, if they want them. That is an evasion, a cop-out. The principle is well established in areas where

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
jurisdiction is shared or unclear, that the federal government indicates clearly certain kinds of programs it wants to have proceed. That, indeed, has been done in this bill. One might argue about the adequacy of the reference or the provisions, but there is specific provision for co-operative housing, specific provision for public housing, specific provision for native housing and specific provision for new communities. If the federal government wants to recognize or establish a priority, it can. But it has clearly ignored the towns and small communities of Canada.
If we are to encourage smaller communities-as I believe a balanced nation must-we will need some major changes. We will need changes first in the attitudes of the bureaucrats whose influence on housing and related policy today far exceeds that of anyone in this Chamber. Whether by conscious act or inadvertence, they have contributed directly already to the decline of smaller communities, and either their attitudes must change or they must be changed. Second, we must re-examine the basis and validity of the projections which we are following now. Once we have some clear view of the future options open to us, we must decide whether we will simply become apostles of the trend and go wherever present trends might lead us, or whether instead we will decide what kind of country we want, what balance we want between large cities and small places, and then shape events instead of letting them command us.
If we do decide that we want to retain the unique values that viable smaller communities can offer modern Canada, we will need, in effect, a co-ordinated national policy on towns and small communities. It is not enough simply to change policies of CMHC, or to amend in some insignificant way the new communities provisions. There will need to be a re-orientation of policy in several fields. The key perhaps will be industrial policy and we will have to consciously decentralize, to smaller places, those light and mobile modern industries which can operate as well in a town of 5,000 as they can on the fringes of a megalopolis. There is already evidence, in the United States and elsewhere, that much modern industry which felt itself confined to city sites can, when necessary, relocate successfully in smaller places.
In my own constituency, a cable plant was set up in a mountain pass community instead of in a city, and the people who work there vastly prefer that environment where they are minutes from skiing and fishing and the out-of-doors. The plants can come and the people can come if national and provincial policy direct them toward the towns instead of in the conventional opposite direction. The DREE policy must reflect a confidence in smaller communities. Government departments should establish special programs to ensure that the assistance they offer gets through to communities too small to hire squads of experts whose specialty is getting government grants.
We need to review our processes of public hearings to end the farce that presently characterizes hearings of the Canadian Transport Commission, to name one, when it pits professional corporate experts against the local laiety and calls the process, democratic. I, personally, would like to see some provision that recognizes how few of our influential public servants have any contemporary con-

nection now with the smaller places their decisions affect. Perhaps a special system of sabbaticals could be arranged which would require them to spend two weeks each year in a different small community where they would be available to the people whose lives they affect.
Without becoming lost in specifics, the point is that any effective policy to make the most of our small communities must involve changes on several fronts. It cannot be piecemeal. It must itself be part of a general community program which aims to achieve the best of our city and town potential. The present bill is an era away from that concept. It is a piece of patchwork, brought forward by a government without goals of its own. It provides no direction for Canada. It is just another vessel to drift in, a little more serviceable than what we had, but almost useless in light of what we need. Mr. Speaker, the sad fact is that the government considers this to be reform. There could be no better proof of its incompetence to govern contemporary Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of this House welcome the amendments in respect of the National Housing Act which are before us in this debate. I would certainly like to congratulate the minister for his part in this legislation and also for the very fine address he gave in opening the debate, as well as for the principles he enunciated which I am sure all members of this House will support. We can welcome these measures as an attempt to achieve what must be a fundamental social objective of this parliament and of this government; that is, to put a home of their own within the reach of every family willing to make the effort to buy one. We ought to see this as a basic right of every family in this country. When we think of rights we usually think in terms of political and civil rights, but as well, we must think of those human and social rights that are equally fundamental to a truly human existence.
We should recall the opening words of the Canadian Bill of Rights, one of the most important pieces of legislation passed by the Canadian parliament, and a great testimony to the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was Prime Minister of this country. The preamble to the Canadian Bill of Rights reads that:
The Parliament of Canada affirming that the Canadian Nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions.
I submit that the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions must include the right to obtain a house in which that family can find its own identity and fulfil its own aspirations. The preamble to the Bill of Rights also states that the parliament of Canada acknowledges the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and the enjoyment of property. We certainly must recognize the fact that there are all too few families and individuals in Canada being given the opportunity to enjoy that last right, the right to the possession of property. For most Canadian families, the right to which this great, classical, historical Bill of Rights bears testimony is being denied them. This right is being put, by economic and social forces, beyond their grasp,
March 21, 1973

and we must face the fact that part of the duty laid upon this parliament and upon this government is taking those measures that will bring that right back within their grasp.
For most Canadian families, the kind of right to which the Bill of Rights bears testimony includes having a house of their own. This is not because living in high rise apartments is, in itself, bad in any way. Such accommodation satisfies many Canadian people who find that it meets all their needs and fulfils all their desires. But it does not satisfy the needs and the desires of the majority of families. They want a house of their own. They want some grass around it. They want a garden in which they can grow things. They want a yard where their children can play in freedom and safety. They want a neighbourhood where they can sink down some personal roots and feel that they belong somewhere instead of being just bits of cosmic dust blowing here and there. They want to recognize people by their names and believe themselves members of the community that has identifiable persons within it, instead of being part of that faceless mass that so often populates the great urban centres of the land. Therefore, these families look upon a house as something more than shelter. It is not just so much real estate; it is something that is intrinsic to fulfilling their full life as a family.
We can, therefore, appreciate the great frustration that so many families suffer, the great despair that they have to endure as they measure the gap between their objective and their possibilities, between an objective which they have every right as Canadians to hold and which so very seldom can the average Canadian family fulfill, for the hard economic facts of Canadian life today tell us that the average family cannot satisfy this desire of its heart. Any member of the House who has done as I have, and I am sure the majority of Members of Parliament have, namely, canvassed door to door through many of our high rise apartments where large numbers of families with children are living, knows that so many of these people feel as if they were prisoners serving a life sentence. They are in and they are locked in for life by the hard realities of economic life as it exists in Canada today. They have no chance to obtain the freedom or the kind of life which they as families would like to enjoy. They cannot liberate themselves from the confinement in which they are being constricted by the kind of economy that this government has tolerated, indeed has so often encouraged.
I recognize that part of the problem lies in the fact that so very few apartment buildings have been built with families in mind. Indeed, were more designed to serve the needs of families, very frequently apartment buildings would be more than adequate, but in fact they simply have not been designed for children or for neighbourhood living. So, we must address ourselves quite realistically to the legitimate hopes of those parents and children who are seeking the traditional right which Canadian families have enjoyed through the years and which all too small a proportion of families are now able to obtain. We must as parliament ask ourselves: can we be taken seriously if we believe, and we ask the people of this country to believe, that this country no longer has the resources to make possible the fulfilment of this fundamental human right?
National Housing Act
I cannot take that seriously and I do not think that the ordinary people of Canada take it seriously when they estimate the resources that are available to Canada, when they look at the extraordinary expenditures of this government, and when they look at some of the lavish spending on projects that have very limited social value. They cannot believe that there are no resources available which may open to the working people of this country a new life. We have to recognize much more seriously that the policies of the present government simply do not open the door of opportunity to the average family seeking this kind of fulfilment today.
We realize the truth of that statement if, for example, we examine the cost of housing in just one urban area in Canada, namely, metro Toronto. In 1971, the average cost of a house was $30,426. In 1972, it had risen to $32,513. By January, 1973, just a few months ago, it had risen to $33,445, and last month, February 1973, it had risen still further to $34,782. The increase in a period of two years has thus been $4,356 or approximately 14 per cent. That is the average cost of housing. It includes the sale of older and sometimes lower priced housing.
The average cost of new housing is higher still, so that a family seeking a house of its own is frequently priced out of the market unless the father or the father and mother between them, have an income adequate to meet the need, and very few families can provide that kind of income. For most of our families, the rise in income that they have enjoyed over the last few years simply has not kept pace with the rise in the cost of housing. The average family is finding that a house of its own is no longer the right that it has been in the past and that it should be now, but rather it is a dream they can never realize.
We see this more clearly still if we extend into the future the kind of price rise that I have described as taking place over these last two years. If the growth in the cost of housing continues at the rate of the past few years, it will mean that the average house in metro Toronto in 1975 could cost $39,000; in 1977, it could cost $44,500; in 1979, it could cost $51,000, and in 1981, it could cost $58,000. Thus, we would have a growth from 1971 to 1981 from $30,500 to $58,000, a growth of over 90 per cent. We can see, therefore, that unless something is done to bring an end to this spiralling, soaring cost of housing in Canada, we are simply going to put the fulfilment of the fundamental family and human right beyond all hope; instead of offering hope, we are sentencing the ordinary people of this country to despair. This is a disaster, not only for the persons involved, not simply for the families who so often say to their members and to others: we would like to have a house, a home of our own. I think equally we must see as parliament that this is a disaster for the country as a whole. It is, for example, a disaster for the economy of Canada.
A massive expansion of housebuilding could mean more in terms of stimulating the economy and creating jobs than almost anything else that the government could undertake. It certainly would contribute much more to the enrichment of the Canadian economy than the handouts and the schemes with which this government has become identified. This "alphabet soup" approach of the govern-

March 21, 1973
National Housing Act
ment will not make the difference to employment and economic opportunity that could be obtained if we had a sizeable housing program equal to the needs of our people I suggest there is probably more spin-off from housebuilding in terms of stimulating related industries than from any other sector of the economy. A dollar spent on housing might have more effect in creating job opportunities and stimulating related businesses than a dollar spent on almost any other sector of the economy. So, to continue the kind of limited effort that this legislation, good as it is, represents is simply to spell the continuation of the economic disaster with which this government has been identified.
More importantly, this would mean a disaster socially. There can be no question that home ownership enriches a family's sense of community involvement and sense of personal stability. If in our big cities we want to avoid the tragedies that have overtaken the great cities of the United States, we must preserve our residential neighbourhoods and expand single family home ownership. The best way to preserve our neighbourhoods and with them responsible citizenry is surely by enabling families to have homes of their own. Consequently, we welcome what is contained in this legislation. We can see the merit of the various proposals that are embraced within these amendments, but they are not going to carry us very far along the road that we should be following. Certainly, they are not going to carry us sufficiently close to the objective that should be before parliament.
We must, therefore, deplore the way that these amendments represent such a puny effort, in contrast to what is a great need. Indeed, they represent such a small effort it is like trying to empty the ocean with a bucket. What Canada needs is a giant housing program. Instead, in many ways the government has offered the people a tiny mouse of a program. As is so often the case, this legislation is another example of the way in which the government gives us the impression that it values very highly what must be an enormous supply of scotch tape. It seems to me that the government is using a good supply of scotch tape to patch up this program and that project, to meet this need and to solve that problem, always in an ad hoc way instead of recognizing and measuring accurately needs and governing their objectives accordingly.
The result of all this, the result of too little, too late, is that the average family in this country is being given not hope but despair, despair that might eventually become bitterness. If this is all that the government can do, if this is all that parliament can do, then it is like saying to the average family in Canada "You are locked in and you will have to stay there". At the present time, only a miniscule number of Canadian families can afford to realize what they want so much-a home of their own. We therefore challenge the government's right to let this situation continue. When we speak of rights, we ask what right has the government to continue this kind of policy? We are prepared to recognize that what the government is doing may not be enough, but we have to ask the government whether it can seriously believe that this is good enough. The government has had enough time in office to introduce a program that would bring much more hope to the ordinary people of this country, and if it cannot do better than that, let the government make room for those who can.

I should like to suggest some proposals that I believe could make a contribution to an adequate housing program for Canada. This program must begin by recognizing that the housing problem will not be solved until we can do something adequate about the cost of serviced land, the cost of materials, and as well-ironically-the cost of money itself. As is so often pointed out by people in this country, there is no shortage of land in Canada. When the point is made that there is a shortage of land for housing, it seems almost an absurdity to people who see stretched before them great unpopulated regions in Canada. But, of course, the shortage to which reference is made is the shortage of serviced land, the shortage of land that is suitable for housing communities.
If we are serious about doing something to alleviate this shortage of serviced land, we must do something about aiding and encouraging municipalities to develop any serviced land that is available for housing and to embrace new housing as a social opportunity rather than, as is so often the case with expanding municipalities, imposing an economic liability upon them. One of the things we must recognize is that a municipality that is expanding its supply of serviced land and inviting developers to build houses is creating for itself a major economic problem with which it is so often unable to cope. When houses are built there are added to the municipality concerned certain enormous social responsibilities with regard to school construction, park development, recreational facilities and the like. So, we must face the fact that although serviced land may be an asset to the family that wants a home of its own, quite frequently it is almost a liability to the municipality.
We must recognize that what may be to some a solution is to others a problem. Therefore, we will not deal adequately with the challenge of housing unless we deal adequately with the challenge faced by a municipality that wants to develop land for housing purposes and provide services. Therefore, I submit to the House that the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, must take steps to assist municipalities and encourage them to expand serviced land that is available and promote the growth of house building opportunities. While land banks in themselves have much to offer the people of Canada, land banks on their own are not enough. Land banks that are just assemblies of land which will not be adequately serviced for community life are really no answer to the needs of people who want housing here and now.
For example, in the early 1950's the federal government, in co-operation with the province of Ontario, purchased the land for the Malvern development, which is located chiefly in the riding of Scarborough East. There was a land bank acquired 20 years ago, before the term was much in use. That land sat for almost 20 years with nothing happening to it, because the land had to wait for municipal services. I cite that example simply to provide some basis for the claim that we will not offer much hope to the Canadian people if we as a parliament say we are prepared to finance provinces and municipalities in the development of land banks that will become available for housing, but do not establish a time frame to construct houses within the reasonably near future. What we need is some solution now, and simply acquiring land is not
March 21, 1973

enough unless we take the next step of making sure that the municipal services will be provided and that the municipality has an adequate supply of the services required by people. We need the roads, sewers and all the other facilities of urban life, but as well we need the parks, libraries, schools and all the institutions and facilities that contribute something to a truly human existence. All this adds enormously to the expense of municipalities involved.
In the borough of Scarborough in metro Toronto where I live, we are finding that the cost of municipal services has spiralled so that taxation on real estate is almost becoming equal to the cost of carrying the real estate itself. It has become a threat to home ownership. In my own case, ten years ago, taxation on my home represented less than 33 per cent of the amount of mortgage principal and interest, but today taxation is almost 75 per cent of that. In a few years, it can be expected to equal that and then go beyond it. This is not because of waste or extravagance by the municipal council or school board; it is simply due to the impact of inflation on these services.
As an example, the Scarborough Parks and Recreation Department budget has increased by 25 per cent over the past four years. This 15 year program for park acquisition called for a further expenditure of $38 million to which interest will have to be added. The same situation can be reported for schools, libraries, health services, fire, police and so on. This means that municipalities and their leaders are often not sure that they are able to afford an expansion of the housing within their borders, much as they may want to open up undeveloped land and make the areas available for families who want to live there. They are just not sure that they can carry the cost. If we go to neighbouring municipalities that do not have adequate planning, we often find that they are put in serious financial jeopardy because they have more families living within their borders than their assessment can support.
I, therefore, suggest that the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, take a serious look at the cost of the burden of housing that has to be borne by the municipalities and the residential taxpayers supporting the municipalities. I ask that the federal government consider establishing a fund that would make a grant to a municipality for such family dwelling structures within its boundaries as are in excess of the number erected the year before. The purpose would be to help defray the cost of community services that the municipality must undertake to provide for families moving into it.
I do not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this fund would meet the need over the long run; I suggested it only as an immediate measure to help meet that need within the short run. The real need of our municipalities in terms of the problem I have outlined, and in terms of other problems that municipalities must solve, is for a major review and reform of the way public revenue is distributed amongst the three levels of government.
We still think of Canada as just a country of ten provinces, two territories and the federal government holding everything together. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is an entirely outmoded 19th century concept. It may have been
National Housing Act
up to date when the British North America Act was written but it is not any longer. Canada is not simply a confederation of ten provinces and two territories; it is to a large extent a league of city states. As far as the largest number of Canadians are concerned, it is becoming that kind of country and will become more so as we approach the end of the century. Therefore, if we today tackle long term planning we must have not only a romantic and understandable desire to preserve our smaller communities and enjoy them to the full, but we must recognize that the largest number of Canadians will live in these massive urban regions which have enormous municipal and social costs laid upon their shoulders.
These municipalities will need a much more sensible share of the public revenue than is available to governments. At the present time, 30 per cent of the expenditures of all three levels of government are by municipal governments. These governments, in turn, can raise only half that amount by their own taxation. We must, therefore, take seriously the need of our municipalities, especially in our massive urban regions, for a greater and more just share of the public revenue that is so often monopolized by the federal government. I would, therefore, ask that consideration be given to this kind of fund which I think would offer immediate and short-term assistance to municipalities and would encourage them to take their full part in the development of housing. In addition such a policy would aid the long term fiscal needs of our municipal governments.
We must recognize that if we are to do something adequate to bring the cost of housing in Canada within the reach of the average family, we must do something about reducing the cost of materials. We could do that by eliminating the sales tax on building materials. This would reduce the cost of the average home, it is estimated, by approximately $1,000. In my judgment, the government has no right to put this kind of tax on materials used in a family home. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) could take the sales tax off candy and pop; we have to ask why he cannot take if it off the family home. Is that a luxury? Is it the privilege of an elite alone? Surely, it must be the right of every Canadian family that will make the effort to obtain one. During the recent election we called for the elimination of the tax, but I did not hear other parties call for it. If they approve of this, I invite them to take their stand with us in trying to bring down the cost of materials used in the family home. If they are really interested in helping the ordinary people, let them join with us in this effort we have been making for years.

We can hardly wait. As well, Mr. Speaker, we cannot expect much progress in home development while interest rates remain so high. We cannot expect progress in family home construction until interest rates are brought with'n the reach of the average family. Not only must the cost of the house be within the reach of the family, but the cost of the money must be within its reach. The money that must be borrowed and repaid over a long period of time is one of the most important elements in the cost of the family home. We must, therefore, initiate fiscal, policies that will bring homes within the grasp of families, not only in terms of the actual selling

National Housing Act
price, but also in terms of the monthly payments for which the family is responsible. It is often this payment that is the primary concern of the family. The first thing that many people want to know is not how much the house costs, but how much will the family have to pay each month. We must look to fiscal policies so that by a reduction in interest rates, and I think by an extension of the life of the mortgage allowable to families, monthly payments can be reduced.
The difference to monthly payments that an extension of the amortization period can make is shown in this example based on a $25,000 mortgage at an interest rate of 9i per cent. For principal and interest, the monthly payment for a 25 year mortgage would be $215.26. For a 35-year mortgage, it would be $201.96. If we extended that to 40 years, of course, the payment would be down proportionately. If we extended it in some instances to 50 years, it would come down still further.
To the objection that a longer amortization means the people pay a larger total, we must reply that most families do not stay in a particular dwelling for the full term of the mortgage. Their aim is not to have a home free and clear as much as it is to move into a home with payments they can carry. Their aim is really to have a home in which they can live. There should be more consideration given to making available mortgages that the average family can carry. There should be more consideration given to the fundamental realities of family life.
In conclusion, I reiterate the commitment of the Progressive Conservative party to the principle of a home of their own within the reach of every Canadian family willing to make the effort to obtain one. We often hear the famous lines quoted that it takes a heap of living to make a house a home, but we have to recognize that the family cannot do it without a house in which to start. We call upon the government to take seriously the implications of the Canadian Bill of Rights, the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions and the declaration that one of the fundamental rights of the Canadian people is the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and the enjoyment of property. Let parliament take action that will restore that right to all families of this country.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-133 gives hon. members the opportunity to deal with a question which is always extremely important not only to them but also to all Canadians in general.
When we are speaking about the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and its importance it seems that all hon. members and especially those from urban ridings have complaints and remarks to make in the House. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has become a gigantic organization and we can judge its value when we analyze the problems which it has not yet settled.
When visiting foreign countries we can see what kind of housing policy they have. If they have only one-family units we can see that the government policy or the policy

March 21, 1973
of the organization in control of housing is family-oriented.
However, when we find that in certain countries housing is more and more oriented towards the construction of high-rise apartment buildings 25, 30 or 40 stories high, we can say that the housing agency of this country is oriented towards the building of non-family units.
This is why I have to conclude, after over 10 years in the House, that as time progresses the further the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation gets away from a family housing policy in favour of a community policy under which families will be piled up one above the other whereas, in my opinion, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been created first to promote construction of single dwelling houses, not 40- or 50-storey buildings, as is being done in all Canadian capital cities.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should also set for itself the primary goal of ensuring good quality housing. When considering what has happened in that field over the last five years for instance, we unfortunately have to recognize that far from improving the quality of housing is deteriorating from day to day.
In my opinion, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was established with a view to protecting the consumer. Now, with so many complaints being heard from everywhere, we have to admit that the consumer is enjoying less and less protection. This is the reason why I believe that before long the government will have to review entirely the objectives of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whose purpose should be to promote the development of housing in Canada.
But today, instead, we can readily see that this organization, far from promoting housing in Canada, has become a housing control tool. The president of DOMTAR, Mr. Jack Cochran, in his Construction Manual, an excerpt of which was published in the Canada Month magazine, said that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has become-

-(the most controlled and regulated business in the country).
"With relaxation of control as a very real prospect, there is no need for pie-in-the-sky dreaming of futuristic plastic cocoons which will emerge from the scientists' laboratories to somehow solve the 'housing crisis'. Instead, and industry of traditional entrepreneurs will be free to seek out a way to beat out the competition in the market place.
"That to me is a much more efficient way to get more and better housing than for a paternalistic government to step in an take over the responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, to recapitulate the way of thinking of the Domtar chairman, he does not believe in the efficiency of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is using paternalistic methods in the housing field. He would rather have assistance granted to builders to implement a healthy housing policy. Nowadays, the Canadian house building industry is deteriorating instead of improving and owning a house has become an impossible dream for nearly 90 per cent of the Canadian people.
People no longer believe in it because of the policy of this government and previous governments which have not been cautious enough to eliminate the economic
March 21, 1973

causes which have placed us in a situation where the average individual believes that owning a family home has become irrealistic, a dream they no longer think about.
I have here the statement made by the hon. Secretary of State for Urbain Affairs (Mr. Basford) in Ottawa on January 22 or 23 at the federal-provincial conference on housing:
Right to housing-
He was making pious wishes-
-I stated recently in Parliament that every Canadian has a fundamental right to proper housing at a reasonable cost. I said and I repeat here that housing is not merely an economic commodity to be bought and sold according to the whim of the market, but a social right.
The minister himself said that last January. I continue:
I believe that every Canadian can reasonably expect it and that Canadians rely on their national government to be treated with justice and to have an equal chance to enjoy part of the wealth of the nation wherever they live.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) who spoke before me said that the average house in Canada now costs $31,000 and that according to the forecasts of Canadian builders the same house would be worth over $59,000 in 1981. In other words, at the pace things are going, property in Canada will have nearly doubled over eight years and that is without taking into consideration the rates of interest which are part of the cost of a house but are not included in the original price.
Is this what the minister means by good housing at a reasonable price?
It is all very well to voice pious wishes in this House, but no part of Bill C-133 deals with interest rates and, in my view, this is where the minister is misled and where he will never be able to achieve what he referred to in his speech in January, when he talked of a reasonable price for housing.
Mr. Speaker, interest rates have begun to change; I cannot give the history of interest rates for the past 50 years, but on January 21, 1957, the late hon. Robert Winters said that interest rates for housing had risen from 51 to 6 per cent, according to the official announcement which he made in the House of Commons, as recorded on page 451 of Hansard.
So, interest rates were raised from 51 to 6 per cent. Today, Mr. Speaker, these rates are no longer at 6 per cent. This government has allowed interest rates to rise to incredible heights. Here is the gist of Telemedia's editorial of January 8, 1969:
It is not by raising the interest rate on loans from 8i to 9 per cent, as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation did on January 1, that the government will encourage Canadians to build. Nor is it by keeping the 12 per cent tax on building materials that the government will encourage contractors to undertake the construction of building complexes.
And on January 4, 1969, the President of the Association des constructeurs d'habitations du district de Montreal, Mr. Albert Gagnon, listed the government's mistakes in the field of housing. As President of the Montreal house-buiders' association, he must know what he is talking about.

Not one of the recommendations he made in January 1969, more than four years ago, is to be found in the bill before us.
For instance, Mr. Gagnon stated, concerning mistakes made by the government, and I quote:
increase in the current rates of all loans agencies. Conventional loans could readily reach 11 per cent and over;
slow-down in the production of new homes, leading to a shortage;
spiraling of unemployment, a situation in contradiction with a policy geared to a "just society"
rise in rents, which will bring about an increase in the cost of living;
increasingly pressing union claims for salary increases, which will contribute to aggravating inflationary trends;
citizens will be denied the legitime right to live in a decent home, or to own their own homes.
Mr. Albert Gagnon, a former president of the Home Builders Association, formulated recommendations, which were ignored.
The editorial of Montreal-Matin for May 3, 1969 repeats about the same thing about interest rates.
I could quote several other articles, some of which are signed by economists who dealt with interest rates on mortgages.
I have here a table showing that a loan on a $30,000 house, at 9 per cent interest, over a period of 25 years, requires monthly payments of $248.40. I doubt that most Canadians can afford to pay $248.40 a month.
It was all very well for the minister to express pious wishes in January at the federal-provincial conference on housing, but when a man has to borrow $25,000 or $30,000 to build a house or get it built, and to pay $248.40 a month to back the principal and interest, it must be recognized that 90 per cent of Canadian taxpayers cannot afford to do so.
If a $30,000 loan is financed at a rate of 9 per cent, the owner will have to pay $74,524 in capital and interest, which means that he will have paid $44,524 in addition to $30,000. In view of the current interest rate and the booklet on insured loans published by the minister and in which no figure is provided, it can be assumed that the same principle would apply to the construction of an appartment building.
I am afraid that the Central Mortgage and Housing
Corporation would have something better to do than let financiers take advantage of small tenants or owners. Indeed, if a tenant lives in a house whose owner must pay a 10 per cent rate of interest, automatically the tenant will discharge most of the payment.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a social role to play and such a role would be much more effective than the part it now plays.
That is why the minister has not concerned himself with the interest rate in his bill. That is why housing in Canada is still only a dream for all citizens because the federal government a few years ago eliminated the ceiling on interest rates, which has been the direct cause of the

There is another point the minister does not mention in his bill nor in any of his speeches in the House or elsewhere, that is the opportunity to recommend to the provinces in need of housing and faced with that problem to deduct from taxable income school taxes, municipal taxes and interest paid on mortgages. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) has never been urged to do so either.
Not only is the Canadian being exploited when he spends a large part of his income to pay usurious interests, but the interest paid to housing financiers is not deductible for tax purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest these are not only wishes but recommendations that have already been made by members of the Social Credit party, contractors' associations and other agencies involved in housing. Unhappily, the bill which is now before us does not even mention any of these recommendations. It refers to only loans granted to cooperative associations.
The whole bill is not to be rejected outright, but it proposes only temporary solutions which will not settle our housing problem. I would not like to offend the minister but, unhappily Bill C-133 is not the answer to the housing problem because it does not strike at the root of the problem and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is only trying to stop the advancement of family housing instead of boosting it.
It Seems to me that the minister should take another look at the first purpose of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to find to what extent the corporation is getting away from it. I suggest that the minister might render a great service to the people by reviewing the objectives of this agency and putting it back into its original context.
Mr. Speaker, at least Bill C-133-and this is the main thrust of my remarks-could provide for rolling back interest rates to the 1957-58 level. It would be possible for the federal government to do so, as it has the use of the Bank of Canada and CMHC. There is no need to create new agencies, as we have the necessary machinery in the House of Commons. We only have to use it, to put the Bank of Canada at the service of CMHC so that we can get loans at lower interest rates for the benefit of Canadian families.
Indeed, imposing 10 or 11 per cent interest rates on 30-year loans is not doing a service to the Canadian people, and neither is the 12 per cent sales tax on building materials. The government talks about unemployment and at the same time it says that we must put the economy back on the track. However, everything it does, through interest rates and taxes, tends to stifle the economic system, paralyze the housing industry, squeeze the taxpayer and dispossess the tenant and the owner.

Mr. Speaker, there is little proof, judging from recent statements by the minister responsible for housing, or from housing

legislation recently introduced in the Commons, that the government understands the current housing situation in Canada. Because the government does not understand the current situation, no concrete steps have been taken to alleviate the housing mess in this country.
For example, the Throne Speech promised amendments to the National Housing Act which would enable a person earning $100 a week to buy a house for $90 a month, and that grants would be made to homeowners to fix up buildings. This plan to subsidize monthly payments for low-income home buyers looks as though it will enable many people, who could not otherwise purchase a home, to do so. But is this really so? After all, when the federal government subsidizes monthly principal, interest and mortgage payments to bring them down to $90 a month for low-income families, that will not enable a person to purchase a $40,000 house, and that is the average price of a new house in metropolitan Toronto today. What type of housing, then, are these persons eligible for? Land is so expensive in Toronto that in 1970 it made up 35 per cent of the cost of a new NHA bungalow.
I would like to suggest that the federal government should proceed with further projects such as were undertaken in Winnipeg. The Housebuilders' Association of Winnipeg and the University of Winnipeg's Institute of Urban Studies have together begun a program to build three houses in areas where only one stood previously. These houses are located in the lower income core of the city. In this area, 20 per cent of the land is vacant, and 23 per cent of the houses are too run down to renovate. The new buildings to which I refer are single family detached houses, with their own entrances and their own small yards, providing the basic shelter that most people desire. The first of these houses was recently offered for sale at $13,000, with a down payment of $600, and monthly payments on a 40-year mortgage of around $84, not including taxes. A similar project is being planned for parts of Toronto by the Ontario Housing Corporation. It appears obvious to me that the federal government should consider the feasibility of encouraging projects such as these in all the large urban centres in Canada.
In dealing with the housing crisis in Canada, the government would be wise to listen more attentively to the demands of the municipal and provincial governments. The minister would also do well to listen to the advice being offered by the people who are building the houses. Many developers feel that single family housing could be provided in many urban areas at half the present price, if only they were given the co-operation of the various governments in place of the many current restrictions they encounter. The project in Winnipeg to which I have just alluded is not subject to a great many other restrictions that are in effect in most Canadian cities. Because of this, it is possible to sell a house for $13,000.
Developers maintain that if the provincial governments financed water and sewer services for privately held land that is ready for development, this would flood the market with serviced land and would drive down the prices on serviced lots. Developers also say that if governments relaxed their long list of restrictions on new subdivisions, such as minimum lot sizes, stipulations as to the type of building materials, and the requirement of elaborate local
March 21, 1973

servicing, prices would go still lower. The federal tax on building materials is also a factor in the high cost of housing. The 11 per cent tax is particularly hard on the small contractors and building companies for it prevents them from competing with the larger developers.
